Consulted
kon-SUL-ted
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Latin consultare, to deliberate, frequentative of consulere, to take counsel. Webster 1828: asked advice of; deliberated together. The Gospels use it twice of the chief priests deliberating a murder, and Chronicles once of a king deliberating a choir.

Biblical Definition

The same verb serves two councils with opposite objects. Matthew records the Sanhedrin’s deliberation: consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him (Matthew 26:4). John records a second and stranger one, provoked by an inconvenient miracle: the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death (John 12:10) — a man raised from the dead was evidence, and the solution proposed was to kill him again. Deliberation is not virtue; it is only a method, and it will serve any end. Against that, Chronicles records Jehoshaphat facing an invading army: when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever (2 Chronicles 20:21). A war council that produces a choir. And Nehemiah, confronting usury among the returned exiles, deliberates alone before acting: Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers (Nehemiah 5:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONSULT as to seek the opinion or advice of another; to ask advice of; to deliberate together; to take counsel in order to form a plan.

expand to see more

CONSULT, v.i. — To seek the opinion or advice of another, by a statement of facts and suitable inquiries.

To take counsel together; to seek opinions and information by mutual discussion.

CONSULT, v.t. — To ask advice of; to seek the opinion of, as a guide to conduct.

To plan, devise or contrive; as, to consult the ruin of a state.

Latin consultare, frequentative of consulo, to take counsel — the root of counsel and consul.

Key Scripture

Matthew 26:4 — "And consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him."

John 12:10 — "But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death;"

2 Chronicles 20:21 — "And when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever."

Nehemiah 5:7 — "Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers, and said unto them, Ye exact usury, every one of his brother."

Modern Corruption

John 12:10 shows a council responding to unanswerable evidence by proposing to destroy it, which is the standing behaviour of unbelief and not a failure of information.

expand to see more

Lazarus was alive, publicly known, and had been four days dead. The chief priests did not dispute the fact; the previous chapter records them acknowledging that this man does many miracles (John 11:47). Their deliberation was about the consequence — that many of the Jews went away and believed — and their proposal was to kill the evidence. This is the clearest case in Scripture that unbelief is moral rather than evidential. Our Lord had said as much in the parable: neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31), and here the parable is enacted by the men who heard it. The apologetic consequence is worth stating plainly. Evidence has its proper use and Scripture appeals to it constantly; but no accumulation of it converts a will that has decided, and the new birth is not the conclusion of an argument.

2 Chronicles 20 is the best answer in Scripture to the charge that faith is passivity. Jehoshaphat proclaimed a fast, gathered the nation, prayed a prayer that rehearses the covenant and ends neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee (2 Chronicles 20:12), received a word through Jahaziel, consulted with the people, and then appointed singers to go out before the army. He did not stay home; the army marched. What he did was order the campaign around the conviction that the battle was God’s, and the singers went first. The Reformed doctrine of providence has always insisted on the use of means, and this chapter shows means employed by a man who had genuinely stopped relying on them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sumbouleuo (G4823), to take counsel together; bouleuo (G1011), to deliberate or resolve; Hebrew yaats (H3289), to advise or counsel; malak (H4427), to take counsel with oneself.

expand to see more

Greek sumbouleuo (G4823) — to take counsel together; the Sanhedrin’s deliberation (Matthew 26:4).

Greek bouleuo (G1011) — to deliberate, to resolve upon; the plan against Lazarus (John 12:10).

Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to advise, to counsel; when he had consulted with the people (2 Chronicles 20:21).

Hebrew malak (H4427) — to consult or take counsel with oneself; Then I consulted with myself (Nehemiah 5:7).

Hebrew hadrath qodesh — the beauty of holiness; what Jehoshaphat’s singers were appointed to praise.

Usage

"Consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him (Matthew 26:4) — deliberation is a method, and it will serve any end."

"The chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death (John 12:10) — the proposal was to kill the evidence."

"When he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD (2 Chronicles 20:21) — a war council that produced a choir."
